method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Confirm it is ethanol, not a toxic alcohol** — methanol and ethylene glycol cause severe toxicity in small doses.
claims.source_text: Clarify if the type of alcohol ingested is ethanol or toxic alcohol as toxic alcohol (methanol/ethylene glycol) can cause severe toxicity in small doses
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Exploratory ethanol ingestion in children under 6 usually causes minor symptoms**, but ⚠️ **infants and young children are prone to profound hypoglycaemia, coma and hypothermia** even after small amounts.
claims.source_text: Exploratory ethanol ingestion (as opposed to toxic alcohol) by children less than 6 years of age typically results in minor symptoms … Infants and young children are prone to profound hypoglycaemia, coma, and hypothermia, despite ingesting relatively small amounts of ethanol
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Even with a raised blood alcohol, always consider more dangerous causes of a decreased conscious state**, including head injury and other drugs.
claims.source_text: Even with a raised blood alcohol level, always consider potentially more dangerous contributors to decreased conscious state (including head Injury ingestion of other drugs)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Household products can be highly concentrated:** perfumes and colognes over 60% · some hand sanitisers 60–70% · aftershaves 80% · some mouthwashes 25% · methylated spirit 95% (no methanol in Australian preparations). Spirits are 45%.
claims.source_text: Spirits 45% … Perfumes & colognes >60% Hand sanitisers (some) 60-70% Aftershaves 80% Mouth washes (some) 25% Methylated spirit 95% (No methanol in Australian preparations)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Units: a BAC of 0.05% = 0.05 g/100 mL = 11 mmol/L.** Peak BAC is at about 90 minutes; it usually falls by 0.01–0.02% per hour.
claims.source_text: eg 0.05% = 0.05 g / 100 mL blood = 11 mmol/L … Peak BAC occurs 90 minutes after ingestion … In most cases, BAC decreases by 0.01% to 0.02% per hour after ingestion
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **BAC effects in non-tolerant adults:** 0.02–0.05% reduced inhibition · 0.05–0.10% impaired judgement · 0.10–0.15% gait and balance difficulty · 0.15–0.25% lethargy · ⚠️ **0.30% coma · 0.40% respiratory depression.**
claims.source_text: CNS effects of blood alcohol concentration (BAC) on non-tolerant adults by BAC … 0.02 - 0.05% Decreased inhibition, diminished fine motor coordination 0.05% - 0.10% Impaired judgement, impaired coordination 0.10% - 0.15% Difficulty with gait and balance 0.15% - 0.25% Lethargy, difficulty sitting upright without assistance 0.30% Coma in the non-habituated drinker 0.40% Respiratory depression
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ask about:** amount and type of alcohol · other drugs · **trauma, especially head injury** · progression of neurological depression suggesting intracranial pathology · cold exposure · drink spiking (eg GHB) · ⚠️ **possible sexual activity or assault** needing emergency contraception or forensic evaluation.
claims.source_text: Other drug ingestion (eg recreational drugs, medications, other deliberate overdose) Trauma / injury, especially trauma to head Level of neurological depression, and progression of symptoms which could suggest evolving intracranial pathology Exposure to cold environment Ethanol drinks can be spiked with other drugs such as gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB) Possibility of unplanned sexual activity / assault requiring emergency contraception or forensic evaluation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hypotension and tachycardia** can come from vasodilation or volume loss (eg vomiting); **hypothermia** from vasodilation or cold; **hypoglycaemia** can lower the conscious state.
claims.source_text: Hypotension and tachycardia may occur as a result of ethanol-induced peripheral vasodilation, or secondary to volume loss, eg from vomiting Hypothermia may occur due to vasodilatation and / or prolonged exposure to cold environment Hypoglycaemia can cause decreased conscious state
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use a lower threshold to investigate infants and young children** — their signs of intoxication are harder to read. **Mild symptoms only:** consider BAC and blood glucose.
claims.source_text: Consider a lower threshold for investigation in infants and young children as neurological and behavioural signs of intoxication may be harder to interpret If only mild symptoms (decreased inhibition, slight incoordination) consider blood alcohol concentration (BAC) and blood glucose
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **More than mild, or not improving after two hours:** blood glucose, U&E, acid–base, ECG if polydrug overdose is possible, and **CT brain if the conscious state is decreased or deteriorating.**
claims.source_text: If more than mild symptoms or symptoms not improving or worsening after two hours, the following investigations should be arranged: Blood glucose U&E Acid base (metabolic acidosis) ECG if any consideration of poly drug overdose Consider CT brain if decreased conscious state / conscious state deteriorating
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **BAC should ideally be done in everyone admitted.** After a motor vehicle accident, state law may require a police-sample BAC.
claims.source_text: BAC should ideally be done in all patients who require admission. If involved in an MVA, either as driver or passenger, you may be obliged by state law to take a Police Sample BAC
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Care is supportive:** hypoglycaemia, hypovolaemia, hypothermia, decreased conscious state (⚠️ **it may not be the alcohol — consider trauma, polydrug ingestion, DKA**), respiratory depression and co-morbidities.
claims.source_text: Key interventions are mainly supportive and include management of: hypoglycaemia hypovolemia hypothermia decreased conscious state (keeping in mind that this may not be due to alcohol ingestion: consider trauma, polydrug ingestion, DKA etc) respiratory depression co-morbidities
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Enhanced elimination is ineffective** (ethanol is absorbed rapidly). **There is no antidote.**
claims.source_text: Enhance elimination - ineffective as ethanol is rapidly absorbed after ingestion Antidote - Nil
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Involve the paediatric team** for ongoing medical management and monitoring, or **child protection and safety concerns.** **Transfer** for significantly decreased or non-improving conscious state, or need for respiratory support.
claims.source_text: Need for ongoing medical management and monitoring Child protection and safety concerns … Significantly decreased conscious stage or conscious state not improving as expected Need for respiratory support
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge when** blood glucose, temperature and investigations are normal and conscious level is normal. Adolescents with deliberate ingestion need a self-harm risk assessment and drug and alcohol assessment first.
claims.source_text: Blood glucose / temperature normal / investigations normal Normal level of consciousness … Prior to discharge, adolescents who present with deliberate ingestions need risk assessment regarding the likelihood of further ingestions or other attempts to self-harm Assessment of other drug and alcohol use should also be undertaken
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ethanol poisoning' (Last Updated April 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ethanol_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23
